newsitem.title: UK: British money supply shows economy blooming.
newsitem.headline: British money supply shows economy blooming.

text.p: British M4 money supply grew by a robust 9.8 percent in the year to September, the government said on Friday, providing further evidence that economic recovery is gathering momentum.

Economists said the figures, widely seen as a pointer to future inflationary pressures, would add fuel to Bank of England Governor Eddie George's calls for a pre-emptive rise in official interest rates.
The Office for National Statistics said M4, a broad measure of money supply, grew a seasonally adjusted 0.8 percent in September, taking the annual rate to 9.8 percent from 9.5 percent in August.
The Treasury said special factors, such as the takeover of building societies by banks, made it difficult to assess the underlying trend, but City economists said the figures were worrying.
"It's another indicator that the economy is picking up," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr. "M4 money supply continues to support Eddie George's case for an interest rate rise."

M4, which comprises notes and coins in circulation, personal and commercial bank deposits and certificates of deposit, has been at or above the government's three to nine percent target range since last November.
Recent official statistics, such as the sharp drop to a five-year low in September unemployment, have pointed to a healthy recovery in Britain's economy.
But other figures, including a four percent rise in July average earnings, suggest inflation pressures could be building.
"The M4 figures are worrying in that they are pointing in the same direction as figures for the real economy," said Schroders economist David Philpotts.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke has cut interest rates four times since last December to their present 5.75 percent level, giving millions of home-owners their lowest mortgage rates for 30 years.
With an election looming by May 1997, he has a strong political incentive to resist the central bank's pressure for an increase.

"This rise, coming with other data showing the economy is moving up one or two gears, will make the Bank of England even more twitchy about tightening monetary policy," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
Bank and building society lending grew somewhat less than expected in September, rising by 3.5 billion sterling ($5.5 billion), the weakest rise since August last year.
Mortgage lending by building societies also fell slightly last month, but economists said the recovery in the housing market remained intact.
The British Bankers' Association ssaid consumer credit growth slowed slightly in September from recent months, as did total lending by British banks.
